lessons.title: Modulus and its graph
lessons.summary: Interpret modulus as distance and sketch the two straight branches of a linear modulus.
lessons.objective: Find the corner, intercepts, branch equations and range of a shifted or scaled linear modulus graph.
lessons.before: Recall how the gradient and intercept determine a straight line.
lessons.ideas:
\(|u|\) is the distance of \(u\) from zero.

For a linear argument the graph is piecewise linear, with its corner where the argument is zero.

A negative outer multiplier reverses the direction of both rays, giving a maximum.
lessons.method:
1. Set the argument equal to zero to locate the corner.
  2. Remove the modulus separately on each sign domain.
  3. Find intercepts and check whether the output is bounded above or below.
mistakes: Use the argument’s zero, including its sign.
Keep the vertical shift outside the modulus.
A negative outer scale gives a maximum.

examples.title: Locate a fractional corner
examples.question: Find the vertex of \(y=|5x-2|+4\).
examples.solution:
\[5x-2=0\implies x=\frac25\]

The ordinate is \(4\) because the modulus is zero.

examples.title: Read slopes on both sides
examples.question: Give the gradients of \(y=-|x-8|\) on either side of its vertex.
examples.solution:
For \(x<8\), the function is \(x-8\). For \(x>8\), it is \(8-x\).

The left gradient is \(1\) and the right gradient is \(-1\).

examples.title: Test whether the graph meets the axis
examples.question: Does \(y=3|x+7|+2\) intersect the horizontal axis?
examples.solution: Every output is at least \(2\). Zero is outside the range.

lessons.title: Modulus equations
lessons.summary: Find every possible value and test any candidate that arose by squaring.
lessons.objective: Solve linear modulus equations with a constant, another modulus or a signed linear expression.
lessons.before: Recall how to solve a linear equation and use the branches of a linear modulus.
lessons.ideas:
\(|u|=c\) with \(c>0\) means \(u=c\) or \(u=-c\).

Equality of two absolute values is equivalent to equality of their squares.

For a signed right-hand side, the original equation requires that side to be non-negative.
lessons.method:
1. Isolate the modulus and determine whether a sign condition is needed.
  2. Solve both equations obtained from the two signs.
  3. Check the candidates in the original equation and give the complete set.
mistakes: Keep both roots for a positive target when both candidates are valid.
Reject any candidate where the right-hand side is negative.
A zero target gives a single case.

examples.title: Compare two moduli
examples.question: Solve \(|x+8|=|3x|\).
examples.solution:
\[x+8=3x\ \text{or}\ x+8=-3x\]

The two exact values are \(4\) and \(-2\).

examples.title: Use a signed right-hand side
examples.question: Solve \(|x+5|=3x+1\).
examples.solution:
The candidate equations are \(x+5=3x+1\) and \(-x-5=3x+1\).

They give \(x=2\) and \(x=-\frac32\). The second candidate makes the right side negative, leaving only \(x=2\).

lessons.title: Modulus inequalities
lessons.summary: Find accurate endpoints and combine the intervals from the correct sign domains.
lessons.objective: Solve linear modulus inequalities, justifying strict endpoints and separate sign domains.
lessons.before: Recall solving a linear inequality and reading intervals on a number line.
lessons.ideas:
An upper bound on a distance keeps the inputs inside an interval.

A positive lower bound on a distance keeps the two outer branches.

When comparing with a signed expression, split into sign domains or handle its negative region separately.
lessons.method:
1. Find where the modulus argument changes sign.
  2. Solve the resulting linear conditions and intersect each with its sign domain.
  3. Combine the intervals and check each equality endpoint in the original inequality.
mistakes: Preserve strict or non-strict inequalities when stating the answer.
Retain both outer rays where the distance is bounded below.
Only square an inequality when the relevant sides are non-negative.

examples.title: Compare two non-negative sides
examples.question: Solve \(|3x|>|x+4|\).
examples.solution:
\[9x^2-(x+4)^2=(2x-4)(4x+4)>0\]

The product is positive outside the roots, so \(x<-1\) or \(x>2\).

lessons.title: Polynomial division
lessons.summary: Find a quotient and remainder, including for non-monic and quadratic divisors.
lessons.objective: Divide polynomials of degree at most four by linear or quadratic polynomials and check the resulting identity.
lessons.before: Recall expanding products and collecting terms of equal degree.
lessons.ideas:
Write \(P=DQ+R\), where the remainder is zero or has lower degree than the divisor.

Each subtraction cancels the current leading term of the residual.

A linear divisor gives a constant remainder. A quadratic divisor can give a linear one.
lessons.method:
1. Divide the highest-degree terms to get the next quotient term.
  2. Subtract the whole product of this term and the divisor.
  3. Continue until the remainder is zero or its degree is smaller. Expand the final identity to check.
mistakes: Divide by the actual leading coefficient of the divisor.
Subtract every term in the product.
Do not continue once the remainder has lower degree.

examples.title: Check the division identity
examples.question: Divide \(x^2+x-8\) by \(x+3\).
examples.solution:
\[x^2+x-8=(x+3)(x-2)-2\]

The quotient is \(x-2\) and the remainder is \(-2\).

examples.title: Start with a non-monic divisor
examples.question: Divide \(6x^2+5x-2\) by \(3x+1\).
examples.solution:
The first quotient term is \(2x\). Subtract \(6x^2+2x\) to leave \(3x-2\).

\[6x^2+5x-2=(3x+1)(2x+1)-3\]

examples.title: Keep a linear remainder
examples.question: Divide \(2x^3-x^2+9x+1\) by \(x^2+4\).
examples.solution:
\[2x^3-x^2+9x+1=(x^2+4)(2x-1)+(x+5)\]

Since the remainder has degree one, the division stops here.

lessons.title: Factor and remainder theorems
lessons.summary: Evaluate at the zero of a linear divisor and use the result to solve polynomial problems.
lessons.objective: Find remainders, prove a factor, determine unknown coefficients and solve equations with all distinct real roots.
lessons.before: Recall how polynomial division is written as an identity.
lessons.ideas:
For linear divisor \(cx+d\) with \(c\ne0\), substitute \(x=-\frac dc\) into \(P(x)=D(x)Q(x)+R\).

A linear expression is a factor exactly when its remainder is zero.

Two prescribed remainders can give simultaneous equations in unknown coefficients.
lessons.method:
1. Find the zero of each given divisor.
  2. Evaluate the original polynomial at that input. Set the resulting value equal to the given remainder.
  3. When solving, divide by the known factor first and find every remaining root.
mistakes: Use the zero of the full divisor rather than its constant term.
Remember a nonzero remainder is not evidence of a factor.
Include the root from the known factor and list repeated roots once in any distinct-root set.

examples.title: Evaluate at a non-integer zero
examples.question: Find the remainder of \(4x^2+x+2\) when divided by \(2x-1\).

examples.title: Remember the given factor
examples.question: Solve \(2x^3-13x^2+5x+6=0\) given the factor \(x-1\).
examples.solution:
\[2x^3-13x^2+5x+6=(x-1)(2x+1)(x-6)\]

Retain the roots of all three linear factors. The solutions are \(1,\ -\frac12,\ 6\).

questions.title: Sketch an inverted modulus graph
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(g(x)=-2\left|x + 3\right|+4\).

  1. Find the coordinates of the vertex and state whether the vertex is a maximum or a minimum.

    [2]

  2. Find all intercepts and sketch the graph, labelling its vertex and intercepts.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \((-3,4)\), a maximum.

(b) \((-5,0),\ (-1,0),\ (0,-2)\). Join the vertex to the intercepts with two straight rays.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[g(-3)=4\qquad \left|x+3\right|\ge 0\]

The negative multiplier forces every other output below \(4\).

(b)

\[g(x)=0\iff |x+3|=2\iff x=-5\ \text{or}\ x=-1\]\[g(0)=4-2(3)=-2\]

Draw the left ray with gradient \(2\) and the right ray with gradient \(-2\) from \((-3,4)\).
questions.hint_html: Find the corner before setting the output equal to zero.

marking_criteria.description_html: Sets the expression inside the modulus equal to zero.
Vertex \((-3,4)\) and maximum.
Solves the positive-distance condition on both sides of the corner.
Both horizontal intercepts.
Vertical intercept.
Two straight rays meeting at the labelled corner and passing through the labelled intercepts.

questions.title: A modulus minimum above the axis
questions.prompt_html:
The curve has equation \(y=|4x-7|+3\).

  1. State the minimum value and the corresponding \(x\)-coordinate. Give the complete range.

    [3]

  2. Find the coordinates of both intersections with the horizontal line \(y=11\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[4x-7=0\implies x=\frac74\]

Here the modulus is zero. Every other input gives a positive modulus, so \(y\in[3,\infty)\).

(b)

\[|4x-7|=8\implies 4x-7=8\ \text{or}\ 4x-7=-8\]

The abscissae are \(-\frac14\) and \(\frac{15}{4}\). Use the given common ordinate \(11\).
questions.hint_html: Set the modulus argument equal to zero to locate the corner.

marking_criteria.description_html: Sets the linear modulus argument equal to zero.
Minimum and its position.
Full range with the endpoint included.
Isolates the modulus and treats both signs.
Both exact coordinate pairs.

questions.title: Reconstruct a modulus graph from two points
questions.prompt_html:
The graph \(y=k|x-h|+j\) has vertex \((-2,5)\) and passes through \((4,-13)\).

  1. Find the values of \(h\), \(j\) and \(k\).

    [3]

  2. Find the width between the intersections with \(y=-4\), measured in the \(x\)-direction.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[-13=k|4+2|+5=6k+5\]

The vertex fixes \(h=-2\) and \(j=5\). Substitution gives \(k=-3\).

(b)

\[-3|x+2|+5=-4\iff |x+2|=3\]

The solutions \(x=-5\) and \(x=1\) differ by \(6\).
questions.hint_html: The negative ordinate of the second point tells you which way the rays extend.

marking_criteria.description_html: Correct vertex parameters.
Substitutes the given point into the model.
Correct signed multiplier.
Obtains the correct horizontal distance from the vertex.
Correct total width.

questions.title: Check both candidates against the line
questions.prompt_html:
Consider \(\left|{3 x + 4}\right|=5 x - 2\).

  1. Write the necessary inequality for \(x\) and simplify it.

    [1]

  2. Solve the original equation, showing the fate of both candidates.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[5x-2\ge0\iff x\ge\frac25\]

The right side equals an absolute value.

(b)

First require \(5 x - 2\ge 0\).

\[3 x + 4=5 x - 2\quad\text{or}\quad 3 x + 4=2 - 5 x\]

These yield the candidates \(\left\{- \frac{1}{4}, 3\right\}\). Substitute into \(5 x - 2\) and retain only non-negative values.

The value \(-\frac14\) gives right-hand side \(-\frac{13}{4}\) and is rejected. The value \(3\) gives \(13\) on both sides.

questions.title: Two distances on the same line
questions.prompt_html:
Consider \(\left|{5 x - 7}\right|=\left|{3 x + 1}\right|\).

  1. Explain why equating or negating the arguments gives every possible solution.

    [2]

  2. Give the full set of real solutions.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a) Squaring both non-negative sides is reversible. The difference of the squares factors.

(b) \(x\in \left\{\frac{3}{4}, 4\right\}\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[(5x-7)^2-(3x+1)^2=(2x-8)(8x-6)\]

Both initial sides are non-negative, so equality of their squares is equivalent to the original equation.

(b)

\[5 x - 7=3 x + 1\quad\text{or}\quad 5 x - 7=- 3 x - 1\]

\(x\in \left\{\frac{3}{4}, 4\right\}\).
questions.hint_html: Equal moduli mean the two linear arguments are equal or opposite.

marking_criteria.description_html: Squares both moduli and factorises the difference of squares, or splits into equal and opposite arguments.
Explains that the step is reversible.
Solves both linear cases.
Both exact roots and no additional root.

questions.title: Count intersections without squaring
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(g(x)=5-2|3x+1|\) and let \(t\) be a real constant.

  1. Give the number of solutions of \(g(x)=t\) for each of the cases \(t<5\), \(t=5\) and \(t>5\).

    [3]

  2. Find the two horizontal intercepts, giving their exact coordinates.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a) Two, one and zero solutions respectively.

(b) \(\left(-\frac76,0\right),\ \left(\frac12,0\right)\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[|3x+1|=\frac{5-t}{2}\]

For a positive target the linear argument can take two opposite values. For zero it can only vanish. For a negative target there is no solution.

(b)

\[t=0\implies 3x+1=\frac52\quad\text{or}\quad3x+1=-\frac52\]

The ordinates are zero because the points lie on the horizontal axis.
questions.hint_html: Isolate the modulus and compare its target with zero.

marking_criteria.description_html: Isolates the modulus.
Correct number for all three cases.
Explains the single solution when the target is zero.
Uses the two branches for the zero output.
Both exact intercepts.

questions.title: Intersect the sign domains
questions.prompt_html: Solve \(\left|{4 x - 3}\right|\le 2 x + 7\) for real \(x\). Give the complete set.
questions.solution_html:
Split at \(x=\frac{3}{4}\). Keep each result in the interval where its branch was valid.

\[\begin{array}{c|c}x\le \frac{3}{4}&3 - 4 x\le 2 x + 7\\x\ge \frac{3}{4}&4 x - 3\le 2 x + 7\end{array}\]

Intersecting with the two branch domains gives \(\left[- \frac{2}{3}, \frac{3}{4}\right]\) and \(\left[\frac{3}{4}, 5\right]\). Take their union.

\(x\in \left[- \frac{2}{3}, 5\right]\).

\[\begin{array}{c|c}x\le -4&- x - 4<2 x - 1\\x\ge -4&x + 4<2 x - 1\end{array}\]

Intersecting with the two branch domains gives \(\emptyset\) and \(\left(5, \infty\right)\). Take their union.

\(x\in \left(5, \infty\right)\).

questions.title: Compare a modulus with a signed line
questions.prompt_html:
Consider \(\left|{3 x - 2}\right|>x + 4\).

(a)

For \(x<-4\), \(x+4<0\). In contrast, \(|3x-2|\ge0\) for all inputs.

(b)

Split at \(x=\frac{2}{3}\). Keep each result in the interval where its branch was valid.
